title: Primary Structural Function
learningObjectives: Describe the member's structural role.
student: What is the primary structural function of the temporary access member in this maintenance setting?
instructor: The member provides temporary structural access across the pit and transfers the technician load to supports B and C.

title: External Load and Technician Weight
learningObjectives: Convert mass to weight and identify the applied load.
student: Identify the external load applied to the member. Convert the technician mass m to the gravitational load W.
instructor: The technician is modeled as a concentrated vertical load at G. W = mg = {{beam_W_N}} N downward. Member self-weight is neglected in the assigned model.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify the reactions permitted at B and C.
student: Identify the support model at B and the smooth-contact boundary at C. Which reaction components can each location exert?
instructor: B supplies horizontal and vertical reaction components. C is smooth against a vertical wall, so it supplies only a horizontal normal reaction.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the force path through the access system.
student: Trace the path taken by the technician load from G to the surrounding structure. Identify where axial force, shear force, bending moment, or contact force may occur.
instructor: The technician load enters the access member at G, is carried through the inclined member to B and C, and then enters the surrounding structure. At section a-a, the member carries axial force N, transverse shear V, and bending moment M.

title: Selected Critical Location
learningObjectives: Identify the assigned section and point.
student: Which section and material point are selected for the assigned stress evaluation, and why must the section carry combined internal loading?
instructor: Section a-a is the selected cut, and point A is the stress-evaluation location. The inclined orientation and support reactions make the cut carry axial force, transverse shear, and bending moment simultaneously.

title: Expected Stress Components
learningObjectives: Select the stress components required at A.
student: Which stress components should be considered at point A, and which internal resultant produces each contribution?
instructor: Axial force produces uniform normal stress, bending moment produces linearly varying normal stress, and transverse shear force produces beam shear stress. The two normal-stress contributions must be superimposed.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Connect model parameters to the calculations.
student: Identify the geometric and loading parameters needed for the reaction, internal-resultant, and stress calculations. Briefly explain the role of each group.
instructor: Mass m and gravity g determine W; angle θ controls global-to-local force resolution; BC, x, and s locate the supports, section, and technician; b and t determine area and moment of inertia; and yA determines bending stress and the first moment of area for shear.

title: Student-Generated Mechanics Model
learningObjectives: Create the structural idealization before viewing the reference.
student: Before viewing the reference idealization, draw the complete access member and a section-cut free-body diagram. Show B, smooth contact C, technician load W at G, section a-a, distances, and local axes parallel and perpendicular to the member. Define your reaction and internal-resultant sign conventions.
instructor: A valid model shows Bx and By, a horizontal reaction at C, W downward at G, the assigned geometry, and N, V, and M at the cut in clearly defined local directions.
gradingNotes: Students should construct the model before seeing the instructor reference idealization.
commonMistakes: Do not assign a vertical reaction to the smooth vertical-wall contact at C.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions defining the model's scope.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real maintenance-access system into the simplified Mechanics of Materials model.
instructor: Assume static loading, a straight prismatic member, a concentrated technician load at G, negligible member self-weight, small deformation, linear-elastic nominal-stress relations, and smooth contact at C. Neglect local contact, connections, technician motion, impact, vibration, fatigue, instability, and material nonlinearity.

title: Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the complete mechanics calculation.
student: List the calculation sequence required to determine the stress state at point A and make a limited engineering assessment.
instructor: Calculate W; solve the support reactions from global equilibrium; resolve forces into member axes and find N, V, and M at a-a; calculate A, I, and QA; determine axial, bending, and shear stresses; superimpose the normal stresses; draw the stress element; and compare contribution magnitudes.

title: Boundary Conditions from the Reference Model
learningObjectives: Interpret the instructor reference model precisely.
student: From the reference idealization, restate the boundary conditions and reaction directions at B and C using global horizontal and vertical coordinates.
instructor: B has unknown horizontal and vertical components Bx and By. C has one horizontal wall-normal reaction and no vertical reaction.

title: Unknown Constraint Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the three reaction unknowns before solving.
student: List the unknown constraint loads for the complete-member free body and confirm whether planar equilibrium provides enough independent equations.
instructor: The unknowns are Bx, By, and the horizontal wall reaction C. The three planar equilibrium equations are sufficient for this statically determinate idealization.

title: Support Reactions
learningObjectives: Solve all support reactions from global equilibrium.
student: Use equilibrium of the complete member to determine the wall reaction at C and the reaction components at B. Report magnitudes and directions.
instructor: The technician is located {{beam_worker_distance_m}} m from B along the member. Moment equilibrium about B gives C = W(x+s)cosθ/(BC sinθ) = {{beam_C_N}} N {{beam_C_direction}}. Force equilibrium gives Bx = {{beam_Bx_N}} N {{beam_Bx_direction}} and By = {{beam_By_N}} N {{beam_By_direction}}.
gradingNotes: Require perpendicular moment arms: the wall reaction uses BC sin(theta), and W uses (x+s) cos(theta).

title: Internal Resultants at Section a-a
learningObjectives: Resolve global reactions into local section resultants.
student: Using the segment from B to section a-a and local axes along and perpendicular to the member, determine the signed internal axial force N, transverse shear V, and bending moment M.
instructor: For the stated left-segment local sign convention, N = {{beam_N_N}} N ({{beam_N_type}}), V = {{beam_V_N}} N, and M = {{beam_M_Nm}} N·m. The signs follow from resolving Bx and By along and normal to the inclined member and enforcing cut equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Do not treat the global horizontal and vertical reaction components directly as local N and V.

title: Section Properties and First Moment of Area
learningObjectives: Calculate A, I, and Q at point A.
student: For the rectangular section, calculate area A, centroidal second moment of area I, and first moment of area QA for the material above point A.
instructor: A = bt = {{beam_area_mm2}} mm2; I = bt3/12 = {{beam_I_mm4}} mm4; and QA = (b/2)[(t/2)2 - yA2] = {{beam_QA_mm3}} mm3.
commonMistakes: Thickness t is cubed for the shown bending orientation. Q must correspond to the area above or below the actual point A, not automatically the neutral-axis maximum.

title: Direct Axial Stress at A
learningObjectives: Calculate the uniform axial stress contribution.
student: Determine the direct normal-stress contribution at A caused by axial force N. Use tension as positive.
instructor: σaxial = N/A = {{beam_sigma_axial_MPa}} MPa. The negative sign denotes compression for the baseline sign convention.

title: Bending and Combined Normal Stress at A
learningObjectives: Calculate bending stress and superimpose normal stresses.
student: Determine the bending normal-stress contribution at A and superimpose it with the direct axial stress. Use the assigned positive coordinate yA toward the upper face.
instructor: σb,A = -MyA/I = {{beam_sigma_bending_MPa}} MPa. Therefore σA = σaxial + σb,A = {{beam_sigma_A_MPa}} MPa, so point A is in {{beam_sigma_A_type}}.

title: Transverse Shear Stress at A
learningObjectives: Calculate the signed transverse shear stress at A.
student: Use the beam-shear relation to determine the signed transverse shear stress at point A. Also calculate the maximum rectangular-section shear magnitude for comparison.
instructor: τA = VQA/(Ib) = {{beam_tau_A_MPa}} MPa, with magnitude {{beam_tau_A_abs_MPa}} MPa. The signed neutral-axis maximum is 3V/(2A) = {{beam_tau_max_MPa}} MPa.

title: Stress Element at Point A
learningObjectives: Translate the calculated components into a differential stress element.
student: Sketch the differential stress element at A. Label the normal stress and all complementary shear stresses with directions consistent with your local axes and sign convention.
instructor: The elementary beam model gives σx = {{beam_sigma_A_MPa}} MPa, τxy = {{beam_tau_A_MPa}} MPa, and σy = {{beam_sigma_y_MPa}} MPa. Draw the axial normal stress as {{beam_sigma_A_type}} and include complementary shear on adjacent faces in the sense corresponding to the signed τxy.

title: Dominant Response and Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Compare stress contributions and make a limited recommendation.
student: Identify the stress contribution that dominates at A, quantify its size relative to the direct axial contribution, recommend one mechanics-based modification, and state at least three limitations of the model.
instructor: {{beam_assessment}}
gradingNotes: A complete answer must connect the recommendation to either the moment demand or a section property and must not claim complete access-system safety.
commonMistakes: Nominal stress at one point does not address contact, connection, stability, dynamic, fatigue, or regulatory requirements.
